blocks.text: One of NALA’s most consequential capital decisions was not to raise. The original product solved a real problem in a low-ceiling market, and Fernandes kept the company small, so no large institutional cap table was committed to the old thesis when he pivoted in 2021. Pivots are often capital crises in disguise: investors hold equity in a business that no longer exists as backed, and the founder must raise while managing old expectations. NALA avoided this by raising its $10M seed in 2022, once remittances had traction. The Series A followed the same logic: $40M in July 2024, raised after a year of profitability and with African venture funding well below its 2021–2022 peak. A profitable company can raise to accelerate rather than to survive, which strengthens its negotiating position; the terms NALA obtained are not public. Headcount grew from 7 to more than 100 as capital went into building the organisation (Tech.eu, July 2024).

NALA’s core needs (product, licences, compliance and its own rails) are platform costs with no separable asset to borrow against, and it funded them with equity. Payments do create one balance-sheet need: corridors must be pre-funded, so money is paid out before it is collected. NALA’s founder said the company “grew faster than we could handle pre-funding”, and in 2026 it took a credit facility of up to $50M for that float, describing it as funding growth rather than replacing equity (TechCabal, May 2026). The facility is a working-capital line tied to payment flows, not a loan book: NALA does not lend to its customers, and how much of the facility has been drawn is not public. The case refines the instrument logic rather than contradicting it: equity for the platform, and debt once a recurring, short-cycle asset (here, payment float) is large and predictable enough to finance.

blocks.text: NALA’s investors suit a global regulated-payments business rather than a Tanzanian startup: Accel, Bessemer and DST bring global fintech experience; angels from Deel, Robinhood, Monzo and Chime have scaled regulated consumer finance in NALA’s sending markets; Norrsken22 adds an Africa focus. Hires from Wise and Currencycloud add similar expertise for competing with Wise and Remitly. The 2026 lender, a joint venture with Japan’s MUFG Bank, adds a bank-affiliated debt partner suited to financing payment flows.

blocks.title: Dilution management and the Rafiki decision

blocks.text: NALA reached 500,000 customers and profitability having raised about $10M of disclosed institutional equity, little for cross-border payments, and raised its $40M Series A only once profitable, which limited dilution at both stages; actual ownership figures are not public. Using debt for corridor pre-funding in 2026 extends the same discipline. Rafiki reflects it too: NALA built its own rails only once partner failure rates of up to 15% became a measurable reliability problem.

why: Benjamin Fernandes started NALA in Tanzania as a mobile money management app and took it through Y Combinator. In 2021 he pivoted to diaspora remittances, later building Rafiki, NALA’s own payment rails. NALA’s capital story is one of sequencing: pivot before institutional money, a modest seed on the new model, a Series A only once profitable and, in 2026, debt for a working-capital need that equity is poorly suited to.
lessons: Pivot before you institutionalise. NALA pivoted before it had a large institutional cap table, when fewer shareholders had to agree to the change.
Raise from strength. NALA’s Series A came after profitability, in a weak market, and still attracted a strong syndicate.

Instrument choice depends on what the balance sheet must carry, not the sector label: platform costs suit equity, while payment float, once large and predictable, can be financed with debt, as can a lender’s loan book.

entries.text: Mobile money management app in Tanzania; Y Combinator. Small early cheques while the original product was tested.
Pivot to diaspora remittances from the UK, EU and US into Africa.
$10M seed from Accel, Amplo, Bessemer Venture Partners and Y Combinator, with angels including the founders of Deel, Robinhood and Monzo.
M-Pesa partnership. Rafiki, NALA’s B2B payments platform, is built after partner rails reach failure rates of up to 15% as NALA scales (TechCrunch, March 2024).

$40M Series A led by Lauren Kolodny of Acrew Capital, with DST Global and Amplo returning, plus Norrsken22, HOF Capital and fintech founders including the co-founders of Chime and Robinhood. NALA reports profitability and positive cash flow over the previous 12 months, revenue up 10x in 12 months and transaction volume up 34x in 20 months (Tech.eu, July 2024).

Secures a credit facility of up to $50M from Liquidity via Mars Growth Capital (a Liquidity–MUFG joint venture), starting with a $25M tranche, to pre-fund payment corridors on its stablecoin-based rails and support enterprise clients. NALA says it still holds more than half of the equity raised in 2024 (TechCabal, May 2026).
